verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection is fatal, and less WAL is a lasting need. The remaining points are fixable. standards-compat-2 and demand-1 ask for OLTP cost and benefit numbers behind the default-on 512-byte threshold. replication-ondisk-1 asks for a confirmed XLOG_PAGE_MAGIC bump. maintenance-fit-1 and standards-compat-1 concern the two record lengths and the changed meaning of wal_fpi_bytes. A committer who knows the WAL insert and reader paths has to sign the record format.

brief.title: Compress whole WAL records above a size threshold
brief.problem: Each full-page image is compressed on its own today, so redundancy between images in one record, or between records, goes unused. B-tree index builds and other large-record workloads write more WAL than they need to. Small records, which carry about half of pgbench WAL, do not compress on their own.
brief.proposed_design: Context reuse for zstd is already committed. The remaining 0001 compresses a record larger than wal_compression_threshold as one unit with lz4 or zstd, flags it with XLR_COMPRESSED and a codec and length header, and falls back to per-FPI compression when that does not save space. WIP 0003 keeps zstd history across records in leased streams that restart at fixed 4MB boundaries so readers can start mid-WAL.
user_visible_surface: New GUC wal_compression_threshold, default 512 bytes; only lz4 and zstd use it.
New GUC wal_compression_streams in WIP 0003, a pool of cross-record compression streams.
WAL record format: XLR_COMPRESSED bit in xl_info plus a compression header with codec and decompressed length.
pg_waldump and pg_walinspect report physical record sizes separately from decoded sizes.
pg_stat_wal.wal_fpi_bytes counts image bytes before whole-record compression and can exceed wal_bytes.
author_claims: CREATE INDEX over 10M random doubles writes about 19% less WAL with zstd and 15% less with lz4.
Records below the threshold are untouched, and a threshold above the largest record restores current behaviour.
In 0001 every record still decodes on its own, so WAL readers need no new logic.
Streams in 0003 cut pgbench WAL per transaction by 17% to 37%, at 0% to 12% throughput cost.
A backend with whole-record compression holds about twice the old compression buffer memory, about 268 KiB extra.
brief.thread_state: Michael Paquier committed the zstd context-reuse parts for replay and insertion in October 2026 but gave no opinion on whole-record or stream compression. Zsolt Parragi is reviewing v13; the author asked for advice on buffer allocation in critical sections and got no answer.
unclear: The proposal does not say how 512 was chosen; the author said it was not based on testing.
The material does not say whether XLOG_PAGE_MAGIC or WAL_FILE_MAGIC is bumped for the new record format.
Surya Poondla's message about page LSN and hint-only records got no reply, and it is not clear which design it addresses.
The proposal does not say whether the wal_compression_buffer GUC from v6 still exists.
No benchmark shows the CPU or latency cost of 0001 on OLTP workloads; only WAL size is reported.

objections.title: Existing wal_compression users get whole-record compression by default
objections.failure_scenario: A site runs with wal_compression = on, which now means zstd first, and upgrades. Every record over 512 bytes is compressed whole, and each backend holds about 268 KiB more. If OLTP latency rises, the site cannot tell why, because nothing in its configuration changed.
objections.argument: wal_compression has been documented as compression of full-page writes. With a 512-byte default threshold, the patch widens what it does for every current user of lz4 or zstd. Message #7 says 512 was not tested. The brief notes that no CPU or latency numbers for 0001 on OLTP are shown, only WAL size. Message #13 shows a low threshold can make WAL larger, so the default is a real choice that needs data behind it.
objections.author_must_show: What OLTP CPU and latency measurements support enabling whole-record compression at 512 bytes by default, rather than leaving it off until a user sets a threshold?

critic.reasoning: The thread shows only WAL size for 0001, and message #7 confirms 512 was not tested. The low-threshold figure is in message #16, not #13, but the missing OLTP CPU and latency numbers for a default-on path remain.

objections.title: Gain from whole-record compression is shown on one synthetic workload
objections.failure_scenario: A committer takes on a new WAL record format, a new GUC and a changed reader path, and the 15-19% saving appears only on random-data B-tree builds. On typical OLTP WAL, whose records are mostly under 512 bytes, 0001 does nothing. The cost stays even if few users see the gain.
objections.argument: The only measurement for 0001 is CREATE INDEX over 10M random doubles (messages #4 and #17). Message #16 says the records over 512 bytes are 0.8% of pgbench records, and the author points to 0003, which is WIP, for the rest. No field report, -general thread or user in the thread describes WAL volume from large records as their problem. Message #6 liked the idea, but did not report a need.
objections.author_must_show: Which real workloads besides random-data index builds produce records above the threshold, and how much WAL does 0001 save on them?

precedents.title: XLog size reductions: Reduced XLog record header size

critic.reasoning: The only 0001 measurement is the random-data index build. "Does nothing" on OLTP overstates, since message #16 puts 47.5% of pgbench bytes in records over 512 bytes, but the thread shows no HEAD comparison for that workload.

objections.title: Compressed records hide block references from WAL parsers outside xlogreader
objections.failure_scenario: An incremental backup tool that parses raw WAL to collect changed blocks meets an XLR_COMPRESSED record. It does not see the block references inside the compressed body and leaves those pages out of the backup. The restored cluster is missing changes, and the user finds this only after a restore.
objections.argument: The claim that "WAL readers need no new logic" holds only for readers built on the in-core xlogreader. Message #36 shows that in-core code already misread the flag, since replorigin_identity reported records as UNKNOWN. The brief says the material does not show whether XLOG_PAGE_MAGIC is bumped. Message #3 mentions bumping WAL_FILE_MAGIC, and no later message confirms it, so a parser that reads WAL would get no loud signal.
objections.author_must_show: Is XLOG_PAGE_MAGIC bumped so that old raw-WAL parsers reject the new format, and how would an external block-tracking tool find the block references in a compressed record?

critic.reasoning: Any WAL format change breaks parsers that do not use xlogreader, so that part is not specific to this patch. The surviving point is that no message after #3 confirms an XLOG_PAGE_MAGIC bump, which is what makes old parsers fail loudly.

objections.title: Split between physical and decoded record length burdens every WAL reader
objections.failure_scenario: A later patch adds a length check or an xl_info test in xlogreader, an rmgr desc routine or an extension WAL reader, and picks the wrong length or misses the XLR_COMPRESSED bit. Tests pass because wal_compression is off by default, and the bug shows up only on clusters running lz4 or zstd with large records.
objections.argument: Message #20 shows a rebase over an unrelated length check (18992dc9d98) that still compiled, but against a variable that no longer existed. Message #36 found replication origin records reported as UNKNOWN because one routine did not mask the new bit. Both bugs were silent and surfaced only in review. v13 clears the flag after decompression, but every record now has two lengths, and nothing makes the compiler or the default tests catch the wrong one.
objections.author_must_show: What makes a future WAL reader or length check that uses the wrong length fail in the default regression run, not only with compression turned on?

critic.reasoning: v13 clears XLR_COMPRESSED after decompression, so rmgr desc routines and readers built on xlogreader see ordinary records; that part is answered. The two lengths inside xlogreader.c remain, and message #20 shows a rebase can pick the wrong one silently.

objections.title: pg_stat_wal.wal_fpi_bytes can now exceed wal_bytes
objections.failure_scenario: A monitoring dashboard computes the FPI share of WAL as wal_fpi_bytes / wal_bytes. After upgrade, with zstd and the default threshold, it reports shares like 845%, as in message #33. The operator finds out from alerts or wrong capacity planning, with no change on their side.
objections.argument: Message #35 keeps wal_fpi_bytes as image bytes before whole-record compression and only documents that it can exceed physical wal_bytes. Today both columns count bytes written, so existing tools read them as parts of one total. The proposal changes what the pair means without a new column or a rename. pg_waldump and pg_walinspect got separate physical and decoded sizes, but pg_stat_wal did not.
objections.author_must_show: Why not leave wal_fpi_bytes comparable to wal_bytes and report pre-compression image bytes in a separate column with its own name?

critic.reasoning: Message #35 keeps wal_fpi_bytes as pre-compression image bytes and only documents that it can exceed wal_bytes. Only the author weighed this choice, so the changed meaning of an existing column stands as a UI question.

other_surviving.title: Fixed 4MB stream restart does not fit 1MB or 2MB WAL segments
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A cluster initialised with --wal-segsize=1 enables streams. A logical slot or pg_rewind starts at an LSN in a 1MB segment, and the reader has to rewind to a 4MB boundary up to three segments back. Those segments were already removed because retention follows the segment of restart_lsn, so the reader cannot start.
other_surviving.argument: Message #17 sets the reset distance to 4MB, which divides 16MB and 64MB segments. initdb also accepts 1MB and 2MB segments. WAL removal, slot retention and archive recovery all work per segment and assume that a reader needs nothing before the segment that holds its start LSN. Under 0003 that assumption does not hold for segments smaller than 4MB.
other_surviving.author_must_show: For segments smaller than 4MB, does the writer also reset at each segment boundary, or which WAL retention rule keeps the segments back to the reset point?

critic.reasoning: Message #17 justifies 4MB only for 16MB and 64MB segments, and initdb accepts 1MB and 2MB. The thread does not say that streams also reset at segment boundaries or that retention keeps the earlier segments.

other_surviving.title: Cross-record zstd streams could act as a compression oracle
other_surviving.failure_scenario: An unprivileged role shares a stream with a victim's backend and inserts guessed values. It then reads WAL growth through pg_current_wal_insert_lsn() or pg_stat_wal.wal_bytes. Smaller growth means the guess matched recent victim records, such as rows hidden by RLS or column privileges.
other_surviving.argument: 0003 compresses each record against history kept in a shared stream that backends lease. Message #16 says a backend taking over a lease restarts the stream for now, and the author intends to remove that restart. Message #35 says a writer resets only when it acquires a different slot. Once history spans backends, WAL size depends on other sessions' data, and any role can observe WAL size. The proposal does not treat this as a security property.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Does 0003 guarantee that compressor history never spans records from different backends or roles, and will that rule hold in the planned design where a new lessee does not restart the stream?

critic.reasoning: In v12 a writer resets its compressor when it takes a different slot, so history does not span backends and the scenario cannot happen today. Message #16 states the intent to remove that restart, so the question stands for the planned design of WIP 0003.

other_surviving.title: Stream compression makes every future WAL reader use a new start API
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A new WAL consumer, in core or in an extension, starts reading at an LSN with the old begin-read call, or a new record type is read by stored LSN the way twophase reads PREPARE. With streams enabled, that record refuses to decompress, and the failure shows up on production clusters using streams, which are off by default in tests.
other_surviving.argument: Message #17 lists five readers already switched to XLogBeginReadStreamed() and an exclusion rule defined as a property: records read by LSN without replay must stay standalone. Future rmgr and reader authors must know that rule, and no list or check enforces it. Because streams are off by default, the regression suite does not exercise the case. The 4MB rewind also adds reader cost and memory that message #35 still calls open.
other_surviving.author_must_show: How would a new record type read by stored LSN, or a new reader using the old start call, be caught before release when streams are off by default?

critic.reasoning: Message #17 says a record without a seen stream start refuses to decompress, so the failure is loud, but only at run time with streams on. Nothing in the thread makes a missing exclusion or an old start call fail in the default test run.

refuted.title: Stream exclusion rule for LSN-addressed records has no enforcement
refuted.failure_scenario: A later patch adds code that reads a stored record by LSN, as twophase.c does for PREPARE. The author does not add the new record type to the 0003 exclusion list. With streams on, the read fails with a decompression error during recovery or at COMMIT PREPARED time on a production system.
refuted.argument: Message #16 states the rule as a property: anything read by LSN without replaying what comes before it must stay readable on its own. Today only checkpoint, PREPARE and XLOG_SWITCH are listed. Nothing at insert time checks that a record later fetched by LSN was written without stream history. The failure only appears with wal_compression_streams on, which tests would not exercise by default.
refuted.author_must_show: What mechanism makes a new reader of LSN-addressed records fail in testing, not in production, when its record type is missing from the exclusion list?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-3, which covers the same unenforced exclusion rule together with the new start call.

refuted.title: No committer has taken on whole-record or stream compression
refuted.failure_scenario: The record-format change is committed, and a recovery or pg_rewind bug in decompression is reported a year later. No committer knows the new insert and reader paths well enough to judge a fix, so the report waits.
refuted.argument: Michael Paquier committed only the context-reuse parts and said in message #25 that he had no opinion on whole-record or stream compression. The author asked twice for advice on buffer allocation in critical sections (messages #26 and #30), and the material shows no answer. The remaining reviewers in messages #33 and #36 work at code level, and none of them has weighed in on the format or on reader design.
refuted.author_must_show: Which committer familiar with xloginsert.c and xlogreader.c has agreed that the record format and the allocation strategy are acceptable?

critic.reasoning: Fujii Masao, a committer and listed CF reviewer, gave design-level review in messages #6 and #11, and the author adopted his suggestion to keep per-FPI compression. Michael Paquier is active in the thread, and weak committability alone is not a design flaw.

refuted.title: Default threshold puts unmeasured CPU cost on every compression user
refuted.failure_scenario: A site with wal_compression = on, which now selects zstd first, upgrades and finds that every record over 512 bytes is flattened and compressed in the insert path. OLTP latency rises, and the operator has no measurement to judge whether the WAL saving is worth it.
refuted.argument: The default of 512 was not based on testing (message #7). The only 0001 numbers are WAL size for CREATE INDEX (messages #4 and #17), and none show CPU or latency on OLTP. Message #20 notes that "on" now reaches zstd first, so the new path is on by default for many sites. A 0003 cost of up to 12% tps (message #17) shows that this cost is real enough to measure.
refuted.author_must_show: What CPU and latency cost does 0001 add on pgbench or a similar OLTP workload at the default threshold, and how was 512 chosen?

precedents.title: XLog size reductions: Reduced XLog record header size

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-2. The 12% tps figure comes from the 0003 stream lease, a different mechanism, and P8 concerned the size of a gain, so neither supports this point.

refuted.title: Default threshold puts unmeasured costs on every lz4 and zstd user
refuted.failure_scenario: An installation with wal_compression = on now gets zstd, so whole-record compression starts at the default 512-byte threshold. Each backend holds about 268 KiB more memory, and pg_stat_wal shows wal_fpi_bytes above wal_bytes. The operator learns about the CPU or latency cost only after upgrading.
refuted.argument: Message #20 says "on" now picks zstd first, so the default threshold reaches users who never asked for whole-record compression. Messages #16 and #17 report doubled buffer memory. Message #35 changes what wal_fpi_bytes means. The author says 512 was not tested (message #7), and the brief notes there is no CPU or latency benchmark for 0001 on OLTP, so the cost to non-beneficiaries is unknown.
refuted.author_must_show: What CPU, latency and memory cost does the default threshold add on an OLTP workload that gains no WAL saving from 0001?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-2 for the unmeasured default cost and of standards-compat-1 for the wal_fpi_bytes change.

touch_points.label: on-disk format / pg_upgrade
touch_points.reason: The WAL record format gains the XLR_COMPRESSED bit and a compression header, and 0003 adds 4MB stream restart points.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: Recovery, logical decoding, pg_rewind and pg_waldump must read compressed records; 0003 changes where a reader may start.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: xlogreader.h and xlogrecord.h change, and 0003 adds XLogBeginReadStreamed() for readers that start mid-WAL.

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: wal_compression_threshold in 0001 and wal_compression_streams in WIP 0003.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: Cross-record stream history in 0003 could make WAL size depend on other sessions' data.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: see objection replication-ondisk-1: Compressed records hide block references from WAL parsers outside xlogreader

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: Every record has a physical and a decoded length, and 0003 adds an unenforced rule for records read by LSN.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: Records over 512 bytes are compressed whole in the WAL insert path for every lz4 and zstd user.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: see objection demand-1: Gain from whole-record compression is shown on one synthetic workload

questions: What CPU and latency cost does 0001 add on pgbench or a similar OLTP workload at the default 512-byte threshold, and how was 512 chosen?
Which workloads besides the random-data index build produce records above the threshold, and how much WAL does 0001 save on them compared with HEAD?
Is XLOG_PAGE_MAGIC bumped so that WAL parsers that predate the new format reject it instead of misreading compressed records?
Why not keep wal_fpi_bytes comparable to wal_bytes and report image bytes before compression in a separate column?
For WAL segments smaller than 4MB, does 0003 also restart streams at each segment boundary, or which retention rule keeps the earlier segments?

committability.owner_note: Michael Paquier committed the zstd context-reuse parts but gave no opinion on whole-record or stream compression. Fujii Masao reviewed the design early. The owner must know xloginsert.c, xlogreader.c and recovery.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a new WAL record format, the decompression path in recovery, logical decoding and pg_rewind, and the default-on behaviour for lz4 and zstd users. The format stays for as long as the feature exists.
committability.author_follow_up: The author has carried the patch through 7 CommitFests and 13 versions, rebasing and answering review, which suggests he stays for fixes.

priority.reason: The gain reaches users of lz4 or zstd WAL compression with large records, and is shown on one index-build test. The patch changes the WAL record format and the insert and reader paths, so the default threshold, the format signal and the stats meaning should be settled before detailed review.

provisional_note: The code was not read. Buffer allocation in critical sections, bounds checks when decompressing, the XLOG_PAGE_MAGIC bump and the GUC contexts could not be checked.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Generic WAL compression
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes generic WAL record construction so that it can compute a minimal edit-distance delta between the old and new page images (using an O(ND) difference algorithm), and falls back to the existing bytewise-difference approach when the result is not short enough. The goal is to shrink generic WAL records for access methods such as RUM, where small insertions or deletions shift page contents and make the existing delta nearly page-sized.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch received only limited review across several commitfests. David Steele marked it Returned with Feedback because it still needed review and did not seem a good fit for the last commitfest of PG11. Open points from the visible review included the author's own finding of a large time overhead in one RUM case, and the request to make compression optional, which the author was still working on. Stephen Frost suggested resubmitting for a post-11 commitfest.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Since the feature does not seem like a good fit for the last CF of PG11
I am marking it Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Tracking the compression effect
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add two cumulative columns to the pg_stat_wal view: bytes saved by WAL compression (size before minus size after) and the number of times compression ran. Users could then compare compression methods such as lz4 and zstd without running pg_waldump.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers preferred to report compression savings in pg_waldump and pg_walinspect, because WAL records already carry the saved-bytes information. Collecting the counters in pg_stat_wal would add code to every WAL record insert. The author agreed to switch to the pg_waldump and pg_walinspect approach, and the pg_stat_wal entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Collecting them in the server via pg_stat_wal
will require some extra effort, for instance, every WAL record insert
requires that code to be executed.

precedents_retrieved.title: Nonreplayable XLog records by means of overflows and >MaxAllocSize lengths
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds checks in xloginsert.c so that the WAL insertion API cannot assemble a record larger than xlogreader can read (MaxAllocSize, later a fixed 1020 MiB limit), and cannot overflow xl_tot_len through repeated XLogRegisterData() calls. It also documents the record size limit in the XLogRecord spec.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier committed part of the patch, the API changes and the uint16 block data checks. He then asked for a rebase of the rest, and the author did not reply for two commitfests, so the entry was returned with feedback. After it was closed, Andres Freund noted that the new record-too-large ERROR usually happens inside a critical section and so becomes a PANIC. He suggested building large records such as the commit record before the critical section.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
No replies after 4 weeks, so I have marked this entry as returned
with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Adding CommandID to heap xlog records
precedents_retrieved.authors: Anastasia Lubennikova (lubennikovaav), Matthias van de Meent (mmeent)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds the CommandId of the modifying command to heap insert, multi-insert, update and delete WAL records, so that systems that rebuild pages from WAL (such as Neon) or replicas that run part of a primary's transaction can see per-command visibility. A later version made the CommandId optional under a new wal_level = remote and moved the rmgr-specific xl_info bits into a separate field in the WAL record header.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the change adds a significant cost for very few users and asked for evidence otherwise. The author replied with a reworked patch set and pgbench numbers, but Bruce Momjian noted the patch had grown much larger. The patch then stopped applying, the author did not post a new version after two reminders, and the entry was returned with feedback for lack of updates.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This seems like a very significant cost increment with returns
to only a minuscule number of users.

precedents_retrieved.title: Logical insert/update/delete WAL records for custom table AMs
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add new WAL records representing a logical insert, update, delete (and later truncate) that do nothing at REDO time and are only processed during logical decoding, so that custom table AMs such as a columnar extension can support logical decoding/replication without extensible WAL. Later versions added SQL functions pg_logical_emit_insert/update/delete/truncate and tests using test_decoding.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the patch, saying that with custom WAL resource managers (his parallel extensible rmgr work) it had become less important to him. Earlier, Amit Kapila questioned whether a common heap-tuple-based format could work for all table AMs, and the patch had stopped applying, but the visible messages show no deciding objection from a reviewer.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Withdrawn for now. With custom WAL resource managers this is less
important to me.

precedents_retrieved.title: libpq compression
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds optional compression of libpq protocol traffic between client and server, using zlib or zstd, requested by the client with a connection-string option. Later versions negotiate algorithms through _pq_.compression in the startup packet, wrap compressed data in CompressedData messages, and let a libpq_compression server setting restrict the allowed algorithms and levels.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier marked the entry Returned with feedback because it had been waiting on author for two months. The last author message, in October 2021, promised lz4 support, but no new version followed after Daniel Gustafsson's rebase with a Windows build fix. Earlier review asked for a cleaned-up patch set, a fix for make check-world hangs with zlib, and code cleanup in the shared compression API.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This patch has been waiting on author for two months now, so I have
marked it as RwF in the CF app.

precedents_retrieved.title: XLog size reductions: Reduced XLog record header size
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patchset makes the WAL record header variable-length, which shrinks it to 14-21 bytes, with about 4-5% less WAL estimated for pgbench. It varlength-encodes the record length, gives rmgrs their own info byte, includes the XID only when the record asks for it with XLOG_INCLUDE_XID, and adds an invalid rmgr ID 0 used to detect the end of WAL.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author stopped responding after review. Michael Paquier objected to the opt-in XLOG_INCLUDE_XID interface and questioned the use of rmgr ID 0 as an end-of-WAL marker. Pavel Borisov then asked for benchmarks showing the gain was large enough, the benchmarking was still a todo, and a reminder from Andrey M. Borodin in April 2024 got no visible reply before the entry was returned.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
But at the second round, some doubt arises on whether this long
patchset indeed introduces enough performance gain?

precedents_retrieved.title: Page compression for OLTP
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds transparent page compression for heap tables and indexes inside the storage manager layer (md.c, fd.c), storing each compressed page in fixed-size chunks of a data file (_pcd) with a per-segment address file (_pca) mapping blocks to chunks. Compression is set per relation with storage parameters such as compresstype, compresslevel, compress_chunk_size and compress_prealloc_chunks, and the design avoids background garbage collection.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The thread ended in silence after cfbot reported in November 2022 that the patch no longer applied, and the author sent no rebase. vignesh C marked it Returned with Feedback because there had been no updates for some time. The visible messages show no review of the design that rejected it. In 2021 the author asked whether the patch could be accepted, and the replies only told him to register it in the commitfest.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There has been no updates on this thread for some time, so this has
been switched as Returned with Feedback.

Revert applying column aliases to the output of whole-row Vars.
Reverted commit(s): Ensure that RowExprs and whole-row Vars produce the expected column names.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
In commit bf7ca1587, I had the bright idea that we could make the
result of a whole-row Var (that is, foo.*) track any column aliases
that had been applied to the FROM entry the Var refers to.  However,
that's not terribly logically consistent, because now the output of
the Var is no longer of the named composite type that the Var claims
to emit.  bf7ca1587 tried to handle that by changing the output
tuple values to be labeled with a blessed RECORD type, but that's
really pretty disastrous: we can wind up storing such tuples onto
disk, whereupon they're not readable by other sessions.

The only practical fix I can see is to give up on what bf7ca1587
tried to do, and say that the column names of tuples produced by
a whole-row Var are always those of the underlying named composite
type, query aliases or no.  While this introduces some inconsistencies,
it removes others, so it's not that awful in the abstract.  What *is*
kind of awful is to make such a behavioral change in a back-patched
bug fix.  But corrupt data is worse, so back-patched it will be.

(A workaround available to anyone who's unhappy about this is to
introduce an extra level of sub-SELECT, so that the whole-row Var is
referring to the sub-SELECT's output and not to a named table type.
Then the Var is of type RECORD to begin with and there's no issue.)

Per report from Miles Delahunty.  The faulty commit dates to 9.5,
so back-patch to all supported branches.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server"
Reverted commit(s): Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server Previously, we skipped a checkpoint if no WAL had been written since last checkpoint, though this does not appear in user documentation. As of now, we skip a checkpoint until we have written at least one enough WAL to switch the next WAL file. This greatly reduces the level of activity and number of WAL messages generated by a very low activity server. This is safe because the purpose of a checkpoint is to act as a starting place for a recovery, in case of crash. This patch maintains minimal WAL volume for replay in case of crash, thus maintaining very low crash recovery time.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 18fb9d8d21a28caddb72c7ffbdd7b96d52ff9724.  Per
discussion, it does not seem like a good idea to allow committed changes to
go un-checkpointed indefinitely, as could happen in a low-traffic server;
that makes us entirely reliant on the WAL stream with no redundancy that
might aid data recovery in case of disk failure.

This re-introduces the original problem of hot-standby setups generating a
small continuing stream of WAL traffic even when idle, but there are other
ways to address that without compromising crash recovery, so we'll revisit
that issue in a future release cycle.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found for compressing whole WAL records or keeping compression history across records. [P1], [P8], [P23], [P3] and [P2] are in nearby WAL areas, but none was rejected for a reason that still applies to this proposal. The thread points to no earlier discussion of the same idea.

Two objections only. The record-format change uses a reserved xl_info bit and only needs the usual XLOG_PAGE_MAGIC bump, which the material does not confirm. The WIP streams GUC is not mature enough to judge from this angle.

Objections 2 and 3 apply to WIP 0003 only. For 0001 the main open point is the format signal to external WAL parsers. Message #21's page LSN concern was not tied to a specific design, so it is left out.

0001 adds no new exposure: per-FPI compression already makes WAL size depend on page contents. The threshold and stream GUCs do not give unprivileged users new abilities, assuming they keep superuser or postmaster context. The material does not state the GUC contexts.

Postgres has no existing way to compress whole records or to use cross-record redundancy in pg_wal or the replication stream. Per-FPI wal_compression is extended here, and compressing archived segments in archive_command shrinks only the archive, so neither covers live WAL I/O or standby traffic.
Less WAL volume is a broad and lasting need, so neither objection is fatal. Both ask for evidence that the 0001 gain reaches beyond index builds and outweighs its default-on cost.
